rv.q: As an implicit celebration of big bodies and of varying, deeply feeling masculinities, Sumo is at its most beautiful.

But what’s authentic and respectful may not always feel satisfying emotionally, and “Sumo,” a Ma-Yi Theater Company and La Jolla Playhouse production that opened Wednesday at the Public Theater, rarely rises to the dramatic heights it seeks.
The play is a solid contender, but it doesn't have quite enough surprising moves to rise to the level of champion.
Whatever the script’s shortcomings, SUMO gives us a glimpse of a world most of us wouldn’t otherwise see.
Dring’s writing offers a fascinating, tender, and complicated glimpse into sumo culture in Japan, with nods to its traditional place in society and the reverence it inspires.

Amid these usual tropes about ambition, motivation and rivalries, the author provides a fleeting homosexual subplot that’s delicately rendered in its composition and performances. Other shady though intriguing sidelights on the sport’s sponsors, fandom and dietary issues flicker but otherwise fade away.
Playwright Lisa Sanaye Dring valiantly navigates these complex historical currents in Sumo, struggling mightily to stay afloat in the first act before finally relaxing the oars a bit in the second.
After two-and-a-half hours, I wasn't sure what point Dring wanted to make about this cherished sport.
Ultimately, Sumo is a well-meaning but unoriginal play that I admired more than I enjoyed.
This world is so vividly brought to life that it’s one of the more entertaining Off-Broadway shows this season.
Sumo offers a portal into a world perilously trying to balance traditions with modern sensibilities.
The development of the ideas and the framing is all there, but the drive and force to keep us fully engaged is one battle that is lost.
But it’s just a subplot, resolved almost as quickly as it’s introduced.
'Sumo' is a compelling exploration of dedication, honor, tradition

cn.t: Critics find this visually splendid dive into Japanese sumo wrestling culturally authentic and immersive, but note it follows a conventional underdog sports story framework that limits its impact.
